summary: Describes a method for automatic provisioning of DNS zones among primary and secondary name servers, by storing the list of zones as one or more regular DNS zones that are transferred like any other.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of telling each server about every zone, you give them a list that is itself a zone, which they copy.

questions: how to automatically provision secondary dns zones
what is a dns catalog zone
how do secondary dns servers get new zones automatically
what is the coo property in catalog zones
subtitle: How a list of zones, published as an ordinary DNS zone, lets secondary name servers set themselves up automatically.

tldr.problem: Zone transfers copy a zone's contents, but not the list of zones a primary serves. Adding or removing a zone means editing configuration on every secondary by hand, which is inconvenient, error-prone and different for each name server implementation.
tldr.mechanism: The list of zones is stored as a regular DNS zone, a catalog zone, made of PTR records that name the member zones plus optional properties. It is transferred with AXFR and IXFR, and consumers add, change or remove zones to match.
tldr.outcome: One zone becomes the single source of truth for a farm of authoritative servers. That power is also a risk: a bad catalog can remove many zones at once, so transfers must be authenticated.

facts.label: Schema version
facts.value: "2" in a TXT record at version.$CATZ

today: RFC 9432 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2023, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem With Zone Lists
sections.content:
The content of a DNS zone is kept in sync between primary and secondary name servers using AXFR (Authoritative Transfer) and IXFR (Incremental Zone Transfer). The list of zones a primary serves, which RFC 1035 calls a "catalog", is not synchronized with the secondaries.

So to add or remove a zone, an administrator of a name server farm must change the primary and also add or remove configuration on every secondary. The RFC calls this both inconvenient and error-prone, and notes that the steps depend on the name server implementation.

RFC 9432 represents the list of zones as a regular DNS zone, called a catalog zone, and moves it with ordinary zone transfers. Other uses of remote configuration through catalog zones are possible where the consumer is not a secondary.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a teacher who has to tell every helper about every new student, one helper at a time. A shared class list that everyone copies is much easier.

sections.title: Catalog Zones and Their Roles
sections.content:
A catalog zone is a DNS zone with specially crafted contents. Its records mostly form a list of PTR records pointing to other zones, the member zones. It may also hold metadata called properties. A member node is the DNS name in the catalog zone that stands for one member zone.

The catalog producer generates and is responsible for the catalog zone's contents. The catalog consumer extracts information from it, for example a DNS server that configures itself from the catalog. Consumers MUST ignore any records they do not support or for which no processing is specified.

A catalog zone is still a regular zone and must follow the standards for DNS zones. It is meant for managing a farm of authoritative servers and should not be expected to be reachable through recursive resolvers. An authoritative server may be set up with several catalog zones, each with its own configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The person who writes the class list is the producer. The helpers who read it and act on it are the consumers. Each student on the list is a member.

sections.title: Catalog Zone Structure
sections.content:
Like any zone, a catalog zone MUST have SOA and NS record sets. Since it is not meant to be queried by recursive resolution, a single NS record with the name invalid. is RECOMMENDED. Every record MUST be class IN, and the TTL has no meaning and SHOULD be ignored.

Member zones are listed under the name zones, a direct child of the catalog zone. Each member has a node <unique-N>.zones.$CATZ holding one PTR record whose data is the member zone's name. Putting the name in the record data, not in the owner name, lets any valid domain name be listed whatever its length. The label <unique-N> has no meaning beyond tagging, but it gives a place to attach more records below the member.

A catalog is broken and MUST NOT be processed if a member's PTR RRset has more than one record, if two labels point to the same member zone, or if a known property has an impossible value or the wrong number of records.

Properties are named by an owner-name prefix, either under the catalog apex (global) or under a member node (member-specific).
sections.plainLanguage: Each line in the list is a numbered slot with a student's name inside. If two slots hold the same name, or one slot holds two names, the list is declared broken and nobody acts on it.

sections.title: Defined Properties
sections.content:
The version property is mandatory. A TXT record at version.$CATZ must exist as exactly one record, and for this RFC its value MUST be "2". Consumers MUST NOT process catalogs with a missing, duplicated or unsupported version. The RFC notes that version 1 was used in an earlier draft and reflected the implementation first found in BIND 9.11.

The member-level properties are optional, and implementations may support all, some or none of them:

  • coo (Change of Ownership): a PTR record under a member that names the new catalog the zone is moving to. It must be a single record.
  • group: a TXT record under a member that tells a consumer to treat that zone differently. Its meaning is a private agreement between producer and consumer, and consumers MUST ignore group values they do not understand. Consumer operators SHOULD namespace their group values.

Implementers may add custom properties. To avoid clashes with future properties they MUST sit below the label ext, for example <property-prefix>.ext.$CATZ globally or <property-prefix>.ext.<unique-N>.zones.$CATZ per member. Their meaning is up to the implementation, with no expectation of interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Some slots can carry sticky notes. One note says which list the student is moving to, another is a secret code both sides agreed on, and anyone can add their own notes in a special corner.

sections.title: How Name Servers Behave
sections.content:
When a name server that supports catalog zones finishes a transfer of one, it SHOULD apply the changes automatically with no manual step. If a previously good catalog becomes broken, nothing special happens: member zones configured by it MUST NOT be removed or reconfigured. A broken catalog SHOULD NOT stop a restarting server from serving the last valid member zones, and processing resumes when the catalog is fixed. An expired catalog likewise loses its meaning until it is fresh again.

Name clash. If an incoming member zone has the same name as an existing zone, the new instance MUST be ignored and an error SHOULD be logged.

Removal. A consumer removes a zone and its state (such as zone data and DNSSEC keys) when and only when the zone was first configured from that same catalog.

Label change. If a member's <unique-N> label changes, consumers MUST treat it as a removal, including all associated state, and then add it again as new. This is also how a zone state reset is done.
sections.plainLanguage: If the list gets scribbled on and stops making sense, the helpers keep doing what the last good list said. A helper only throws away a student's things if that student came from this very list.

sections.title: Moving Zones Between Catalogs
sections.content:
If every consumer involved supports coo, the RFC RECOMMENDS using it. The old catalog adds coo.<unique-N>.zones.$OLDCATZ as a PTR to the new catalog's name. A consumer does not move the zone straight away. It waits for an update of the new catalog that contains the zone, and first checks the coo property is still present in the old one.

Without coo, the zone must be removed from the old catalog and then added to the new one. A consumer that sees the new catalog's addition before it sees the removal may treat it as a name clash and refuse the move. Recovery is out of scope, though a manually forced retransfer of the new catalog is one example.

Unless the member label is the same in the new catalog, the zone's state is reset on migration. If it is the same, the new owner can take over the old owner's state. To prevent that, the old owner must reset the state, for example by changing the label, before or together with adding coo.
sections.plainLanguage: To move a student to another class list, the old list says where they are going. The student only switches once the new list really includes them.

sections.title: Security and Operational Notes
sections.content:
Catalog zone transfers are RECOMMENDED to be authenticated, for example with TSIG (RFC 8945) or strict or mutual TLS using zone transfer over TLS or QUIC (RFC 9103). DNS UPDATE (RFC 2136) used to change a catalog SHOULD be authenticated too. TSIG shared secrets for member zones SHOULD NOT appear in the catalog, although key identifiers may.

Catalogs reveal which zones consumers serve, so operators SHOULD limit who can query them. Control over which zones a server serves moves from the server operator to the catalog owner, so consumers SHOULD limit admissible member zones, for example with regular expressions or by checking another database.

The RFC warns that great power comes with great responsibility: a script that generates an empty catalog could delete millions of member zones from secondaries within seconds. It also advises a producer not to use names it does not control, and notes that an NOTIFY for a zone can arrive before the zone shows up in the catalog.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the list tells helpers what to do, only trusted people should be able to change it. If someone hands over an empty list by mistake, every helper might drop all their work.

sections.title: IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the "DNS Catalog Zones Properties" registry under the "Domain Name System (DNS) Parameters" registry. New entries use Expert Review, except prefixes ending in the label ext, which are Private Use. The registry applies to schema version "2".

It starts with five entries, all pointing to RFC 9432: zones (list of member zones), version (schema version), coo (Change of Ownership), group (Group) and *.ext (custom properties).
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps a public notebook of the official sticky-note names so nobody reuses one for something else.

data.title: Member zone records
data.code:
<unique-1>.zones.$CATZ 0 IN PTR example.com.
<unique-2>.zones.$CATZ 0 IN PTR example.net.
<unique-3>.zones.$CATZ 0 IN PTR example.org.

items.label: Schema version
items.desc: A TXT record that MUST be "2".

items.label: Change of Ownership
items.desc: Names the catalog a member zone moves to.

items.label: Group
items.desc: TXT value that signals special treatment to consumers.

items.label: Custom properties
items.desc: Private Use, meaning set by the implementation.
